title: Missing file error when fragment refresh rate is too high
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

When there is a fragment running in the background with a sufficiently small `run_every` value, uploaded files can go missing.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

if "i" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.i = 0

@st.experimental_fragment(run_every=0.1)
def counter ():
    st.write(f"annoying counter... {st.session_state.i}")
    st.session_state.i += 1

with st.empty():
    counter()

image = st.file_uploader("upload an image")
if image is not None:
    st.image(image)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Just execute the code provided. Might take a few tries to get the error.

### Expected Behavior

The selected image is displayed.

### Current Behavior

A zero is written to the UI with the message on the terminal `2024-07-12 15:58:37.682 MediaFileHandler: Missing file 3204b082f9397de0e5b0357c7eb53007c9f5c2abcdfd60fb1c2c7a2c.jpg`.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Python version: 3.10.6
- Operating System: Executing inside docker Linux Docker 5.15.140-release-94a7f6a-81353a4

Thanks for reporting this issue! I have been able to reproduce it. I believe its because the web app sends an update message but since the fragment has not been included in the app run anymore, the fragment id is missing. Probably the right way for us is to keep track of whether an update is coming from the `rerun_every` behavior and ignore the error in that case or notify the web app about the removal somehow, although this might lead to a race condition between the two messages 🤔 

Update:
As a workaround, you should be able to put a `try-except` block around your `fragment` annotated block:

```python
try:
  @st.experimental_fragment(run_every=0.1)
  def counter():
    st.write(f"timer: {st.session_state.i}")
    st.session_state.i += 1
except Exception as ex:
  print(ex)
```

Of course, this will hide any other issues going on as well, so I don't recomment this as a general advice 🙂 
You could also catch the `FragmentStorageKeyError` from `streamlit.errors` to lower the blast-radius of the except, but please **note** that we do not guarantee this to be a stable import path across releases; so the import could change in the future.

title: Enhanced JavaScript File Serving in Streamlit
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

We propose enhancing Streamlit's capability to serve JavaScript files with the correct MIME type. This improvement will streamline the integration of applications such as WebGL and those built with WebPack, eliminating the need for an additional webserver and proxy.

### Why?

Our WebGL JavaScript application, built with WebPack, is integrated into our Streamlit application. Currently, JavaScript files served by Streamlit are set to the content type text, which prevents correct browser execution. This limitation necessitates an additional webserver and proxy, complicating deployment and maintenance.

### How?

To address this issue, we suggest modifying Streamlit's static file server to be configurable to allow:

* Setting the correct MIME type application/javascript for .js files.
* (Optional) Introducing a Streamlit parameter to allow to set or override MIME types for static files.

### Additional Context

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/1567

https://docs.streamlit.io/knowledge-base/using-streamlit/how-host-static-files

I'm the maintainer of Tornado and I've gotten a few reports of this upstream: https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/issues/3373

I've never seen any reports like this before and can't reproduce the problem myself. The one slightly unusual thing that caught my attention when I looked at the streamlit code is that [`BrowserWebSocketHandler` subclasses `tornado.websocket.WebSocketHandler` and streamlit's `SessionClient`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/90dcc14253c4a9dc08aaf899b3bc7c3d004c2946/lib/streamlit/web/server/browser_websocket_handler.py#L42), while [`SessionClient` is a `typing.Protocol`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/90dcc14253c4a9dc08aaf899b3bc7c3d004c2946/lib/streamlit/runtime/session_manager.py#L33). Subclassing a typing.Protocol is a bit unusual (normally you'd either use an abstract base class and subclass, or use a typing.Protocol and duck typing), and it has had weird issues with the `__init__` method in the past. In particular, [this bug](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/31628) was fixed in Python 3.11, and everyone that has specified a python version for this problem have been on 3.10. ### Checklist

### Summary

This issue proposes adding OpenTelemetry (or maybe other if better solution) to the Streamlit library to enhance observability and troubleshooting capabilities for Streamlit applications.

### Why?

- **Performance monitoring:** Track performance metrics like request latency to optimize Streamlit applications.
- **Traceability:** Trace requests across various components of the application, aiding in identifying bottlenecks and understanding data flow.
- **Better understanding of user interactions:** Capture key user events and actions within Streamlit apps, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of user behavior.

### How?

Leverage the OpenTelemetry Python SDK to instrument Streamlit components and collect relevant telemetry data.

### Additional Context

I'd love to contribute to this issue if it aligns with the project's vision.

title: Allow configuring HTTP Security Headers
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

**1. Missing HTTP Security Headers**
While deploying the app using the streamlit, I've found that we can't configure the following HTTP security headers:
  • Strict transport security
  • X-Content type options
  • X-Frame-Options 
  • Content Security Policy (CSP)

Security headers help an application to prevent many attacks like man in the middle attack (MiTM), cross site scripting (XSS), Clickjacking etc. These configurations are important to enhance the security features of the app.

**2. Banner Disclosure**                                         
I also observed that the application's response headers disclose information about the server and its version. Specifically, the header reveals that the server is running "TornadoServer v6.4".
[image]

Disclosing server and version information can aid attackers in identifying vulnerabilities specific to the server software being used, thereby increasing the risk of targeted attacks.

**Possible Solution**
Just like other configurations for the app, these security settings can also be defined in config.toml file.

Hi @user, given that Streamlit doesn't support nonces in CSP headers, could you provide proxy server configuration examples for securely implementing CSP for script, style, and eval, without compromising the loading of the application's visual elements and static assets? I'm encountering issues with 'self' breaking the application, while 'unsafe' introduces vulnerabilities.

Additionally, I've been exploring the option of implementing a middleware server between the proxy server and Streamlit to dynamically inject nonces. However, I have not been successful in getting this approach to function correctly. Has anyone attempted any kind of workaround?

## Update

Exciting news 🎉 Starting with **Streamlit 1.53**, we've added experimental support for custom middleware via the new ASGI/Starlette integration.

You can now configure HTTP security headers:

```python
from streamlit.starlette import App
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

class SecurityHeadersMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        response = await call_next(request)
        response.headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY"
        response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"
        response.headers["X-XSS-Protection"] = "1; mode=block"
        return response

app = App("main.py", middleware=[Middleware(SecurityHeadersMiddleware)])
```

We'd love your feedback on this feature! Please try it out and report any issues in our [feedback thread](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13600).

> **Note:** Requires `pip install streamlit[starlette]`

## Update

Starlette will become the default server in 1.57 which will allow adding security headers as described above without having to install the `starlette` dependencies. The `App` object will also be available in the `st` namespace:

```python
import streamlit as st

...

st.App(...)
```

comments.text:
I have used [cloudflared](https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflared) in the past for that purpose and it is quite simple. Say, for example, you have a streamlit application running locally at `localhost:8501`, then you can tunnel that through cloudflared:

```sh
./cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8501
```

That will return a quick tunnel with a public URL:

``` 
Requesting new quick Tunnel on trycloudflare.com...
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Your quick Tunnel has been created! Visit it at (it may take some time to be reachable):  |
|  https://wings-nurse-cradle-traveling.trycloudflare.com                                    |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Besides cloudflared, there are also some other tunnel solutions like [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/) or [localtunnel](https://theboroer.github.io/localtunnel-www/). I will keep this feature request open. If there is enough interest, maybe we will integrate a native solution into the Streamlit CLI directly.

As of 04.2025, I have tested both ngrok and localtunnel, and they work quite well. A quick-start guide:

+ localtunnel

Run at the same machine as the local server, which is supposed to be accessible on the Internet.

```bash
lt --port 7860 --subdomain your_subdomain
```

Then visit:

```
https://your_subdomain.loca.lt
```

The password to access it the public IP address of the machine hosting the local server.

**Note**: one can create custom domain of choice.

+ ngrok

Generate the API key at https://dashboard.ngrok.com/get-started/your-authtoken

Then:

```bash
ngrok config add-authtoken <token>
```

Run at the same machine as the local server:

```bash
ngrok http 7860
```

Then visit (see url in the output of the command above):

```
https://some_random_domain.ngrok-free.app
```

**Note**: one **cannot** create custom domain of choice in free tier.

title: stSidebarNav items should be disabled when app is disconnected
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

When the websocket is disconnected, input widgets are disabled and show a 🚫 icon on hover. However, the stSidebarNav in a multi page app continues to show a white glove pointer icon on mouse hover. But it is not possible to switch pages while the app is disconnected. Instead of showing the white glove, the stSidebarNav should show a 🚫 icon over its items.

### Reproducible Code Example

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a multipage app
2. disconnect network, wait for input widgets e.g. slider to turn grey and disabled
3. hover over and try to click a page in stSidebarNav

disabled icon on hover

### Current Behavior

white glove pointer icon on hover

comments.text:
Hey @user!

thank you for opening this issue!

At the moment, the implementation details are such that uploaded files are stored in RAM (not on disk), and are available to the streamlit application from there.

Therefore, it is expected that an attempt to upload a file that is almost the entire available RAM leads to the application crash.

I will reclassify this bug into a feature request, for example, the ability to upload files directly to cloud storage (say, to S3, or similar) could partially solve this problem.

Hi,

Thanks for the response.

Are there any known workarounds for this issue at the moment?

@user him, in case of limited resources of RAM, processing large files in the Streamlit app could be problematic because, with a native approach, it would be loaded in memory. One solution I could imagine is to ask users to upload a file into cloud storage (S3 or similar), and instead of file uploader use text input in the streamlit app for user to past File URL.

I have noticed the same problem.

Uploading files via `file_uploader`, regardless of file size, increases the amount of memory used by Streamlit. The server then crashes when the available memory size is exceeded. There is no way to release the increased memory; pressing the x button in the UI does not fully release the memory. No way to release memory from code is provided that I think this function must be need for user.

In addition, this problem is more pronounced when using the `accept_multiple_files=True` option to upload multiple files. This is because it is not possible to limit the total file size that can be uploaded. We can set the maximum upload size per file with `maxUploadSize` in `.streamlit/config.toml`, but not the total file size of multiple files uploading.

This defect prevents Streamlit applications that use `file_uploader` from running for long periods of time.
This issue has been reported [issues/2408](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/2408) but has yet to be resolved.

I'm facing the very same issue here (server killed when uploading 3.5GB files) and I could gather more information about it.

The problem I see is double, and it may point at a memory leak, or a lack of cache clearance as mentioned in #2408:
1. The uploaded files exist twice in the process memory, which means that to upload 3.5GB files you need at least 7GB of free memory
2. One of the copies perists after the script ends running, which means that uploaded files accumulate in memory until the memory is full

To verify it, I created a script (below) that:
- Tells the process memory usage when the script starts
- Lets you upload a file
- Tells the memory usage after capturing the uploaded file
- Deletes the uploaded file variable and collects garbage
- Tells the memory usage after clearing the file

```python
import gc
import os

import psutil
import streamlit as st

def humansize(num, suffix="B"):
    for unit in ("", "Ki", "Mi", "Gi", "Ti", "Pi", "Ei", "Zi"):
        if abs(num) < 1024.0:
            return f"{num:3.1f}{unit}{suffix}"
        num /= 1024.0

    return f"{num:.1f}Yi{suffix}"

def process_memory():
    process = psutil.Process(os.getpid())
    mem_info = process.memory_info()
    return humansize(mem_info.rss)

gc.collect()

st.title("File Upload Test")
st.write(f"Debug - initial memory usage: {process_memory()}")
uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file to upload")
if uploaded_file is not None:
    st.write(f"Uploaded file size: {humansize(uploaded_file.size)}")

st.write(f"Memory usage after upload: {process_memory()}")

del uploaded_file
gc.collect()

st.write(f"Final memory usage after deleting the file: {process_memory()}")
```

And what I can observe is that:
1. Memory grows by twice the file size every time a file is uploaded
2. Half of the memory increase persists from run to run, and it accumulates.

Here is a snapshot of what this looks like after uploading a 1GB file (process memory usage was at 47MiB at cold start):

[image]

And every time I re-upload the file the process memory increases by 1 additional GB.

Ok, after some more debugging I figured out a workaround to fix both problems: the duplicate memory usage and the persistence between executions: In order to prevent the objects from staying in memory you need to
1. Clear the UploadedFileManager session files
2. Clear the session state

```
import streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner as scriptrunner

# Clearing the session files removes the file copy, reducing memory footprint by half
ctx = scriptrunner.get_script_run_ctx()
ctx.uploaded_file_mgr.remove_session_files(ctx.session_id)

uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file to upload", key='file-upload')

# deleting the file_uploader input value after capturing it prevents it from persisting between runs.
del st.session_state['file-upload']
```

Doing it like this:
1. When the file is uploaded the process memory is roughly the size of the uploaded file and just a bit more
2. When the script is ended the memory has gone down to what it was before uploading the file

[image]

Memory overhead when uploading a 1.2GB csv file, the spike is quite insane.

Script used:

```
import streamlit as st
from memory_profiler import profile

# Title of the app
st.title("File Upload Memory Overhead Example")

# File uploader widget
uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Upload a file", type=["txt", "csv", "jpg", "png"])

@user
def process_file(file):
    if file is not None:
        # Convert size from bytes to megabytes
        file_size_mb = file.size / 1024 / 1024
        
        # Display file information
        st.write(f"**File name:** {file.name}")
        st.write(f"**File size (MB):** {file_size_mb:.2f} MB")
        st.write(f"**Content type:** {file.type}")

# Call the function to process the file
process_file(uploaded_file)
```

and then run it with 
```mprof run streamlit run uploadfile_test.py --server.maxUploadSize 2000``` 

I would love a functionality where it could be streamed into /tmp/ folder while uploading

@user I worked around this by replacing the streamlit uploader with a FastApi variant I whipped up with claude. It is a bit buggy with triggers after it's done uploading, but a st.button can workaround that problem. This way the file gets uploaded directly into the /tmp/ folder and the streamlit application can read the file as you normally would with python ( with open(my_temp_file, 'r') as f: ... ). title: ScriptRunContext is not thread safe and causes spurious `CachedWidgetWarning`
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

[This refactor](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/commit/337c0ba548fce197581dacd4582a9a5889b06d25) added a `disallow_cached_widget_usage` field to `ScriptRunContext`. This field gets set and unset as we enter and exit cahced functions. If we add a UI element (ie. with st.foo), and `disallow_cached_widget_usage` is set, then we raise `CachedWidgetWarning`. Because this is done to a global context variable, one thread can enter a cached function while another is calling an st.foo function while raises N copies of the warning for each st.foo call, despite not breaking the rules the warning is protecting.

---

Here's where streamlit calls cached functions, which only happens when we have not already cached the result:`streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_utils.py` `_handle_cache_miss`
```
# We acquired the lock before any other thread. Compute the value!
with self._info.cached_message_replay_ctx.calling_cached_function(
    self._info.func, self._info.allow_widgets
):
    computed_value = self._info.func(*func_args, **func_kwargs)
```

`streamlit/runtime/caching/cached_message_replay.py` has `calling_cached_function` which gets the current ctx and sets `disallow_cached_widget_usage=True`. It has a `finally` block which should set `disallow_cached_widget_usage=False` (unless it is a nested function). Note, the nested function check doesn't seem to be what's hitting us (I naively tried removing it and it didn't fix it).

From `streamlit/elements/utils.py`  we get the current context and check `disallow_cached_widget_usage`. If so, then we raise the warning/exception `Your script uses a widget command in a cached function`.I've confirmed that we hit the `CachedWidgetWarning` *after* starting to call a cached function but *before* we have finished and hit that finally block above.

---

I don't currently have a minimal example. My app is quite large and we use async to render multiple containers at the same time. I am hoping the description above is sufficiently precise to explain how/why the issue occurs.

We ran into a similar issue previously https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7668, where Eric made a change to use contextvars to avoid having non-thread-safe data in `ScriptRunContext`.

I have verified that doing the same flavor of fix (using contextvars to check `disallow_cached_widget_usage`) works.

title: Images do not appear in Cloud Run with concurrency=1
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Images are **not** displayed in Cloud Run when using concurrency=1.
Cloud Run log are "GET 404 208 B 2ms Chrome 127" and "MediaFileHandler: Missing file".
Reloading the page sometimes fix it, but the first display always fails.
Incidentally images are displayed in local machine(M1 Mac).

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
########## app.py ##########
import io
import requests

Sorry, `Expected Behavior` and `Current Behavior` images are reversed.

Hey @user!

thank you for opening this issue!

If I understood correctly, `concurrency 1` is responsible for setting  maximum concurrent requests per instance https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/concurrency#gcloud

therefore, setting it to 1 leads to a request to get the image from in-memory Streamlit storage to another instance where the image doesn't exist. 

In order for this to work, you need to increase the concurrency number (to process HTTP requests) and ensure that the HTTP request for an image lands on the same instance via the "sticky" session mechanism. 

The good news is that if you serve only images from external URLs, you can use that URL directly in `st.image` instead, and it will not affect the concurrency limitation.

E.g.
```python
import streamlit as st

st.image("https://www.python.org/static/img/python-logo.png")
```

Hope this is helpful
Going to close this issue as it is expected behavior based on our understanding of gcloud concurrency.

title: st.file_uploader AxiosError caused by _streamlit_xsrf cookie deletion when popup windows are closed
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

In certain conditions, after a popup window is opened and closed, the FileUploader widget displays and AxiosError:

```
AxiosError: Request failed with status code 413
```

An example of a "popup window" that causes this bug is the [msal_streamlit_authentication](https://github.com/mstaal/msal_streamlit_authentication) component, but this bug can also be triggered without that component as described below.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
# Example using the msal_streamlit_authentication component, which reliably reproduces the issue
# (but requires an Azure account to test)

# Bug can also be reproduced without this component as explained below

import streamlit as st
from msal_streamlit_authentication import msal_authentication

value = msal_authentication(auth={clientId": "", authority": "...", redirectUri": "...",})
files = st.file_uploader("Upload your file")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app and open dev tools; observe that the `_streamlit_xsrf` is present.
2. Click "login", and follow prompts in the popup until it closes.
3. Open dev tools; observe that the `_streamlit_xsrf` is absent.
4. Try uploading a file, and see an `AxiosError`.

### Expected Behavior

The file uploader should work

### Current Behavior

The file uploader displays an `AxiosError`.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.37.1
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Linux
- Browser: Edge (also tested on Chrome). Cannot reproduce issue in Firefox.

### Additional Information

After some debugging, we think the cause is in Streamlit's handling of the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie which is required by the cross-site scripting protection. Specifically, after certain popup interactions, the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie is deleted and does not reappear.

The root cause seems to be this part of the frontend code which handles a changed connection state, and triggers the deletion of the cookie:

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1e107ad84be5b30be6aa25bab127f1edbf0d823b/frontend/app/src/App.tsx#L657

When a new client connects to streamlit from a browser with an active session, it loads and executes `app.js` and ends up executing `handleConnectionStateChanged` logic. When executing it, it begins in a state that is not connected. The logic results in a deletion of the cookie. The normal flow seems to be that the cookie is recreated if the connection is successful; however, if the two cases that we describe below, the window is killed after the cookie deletion but before it can create a successful connection.

So what circumstances causes this deletion? We have found two ways to reproduce this issue:

### Method 1: login popup

The bug can be reliably reproduced using an "Azure login" component, although this requires an Azure account to login to.

The [msal_streamlit_authentication](https://github.com/mstaal/msal_streamlit_authentication) component allows one to authenticate with Azure via a popup window. After the login flow is completed, the popup window URL is briefly redirected to the streamlit app (e.g. `localhost:8501/spa`) but then the popup window it is quickly closed and the user returns to the main browser window. However, the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie has been deleted and the file uploader does not work.

The issue can subsequently be fixed by a user refreshing the page.

I don't think the bug lies with that component. It is specifically the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie and no other cookies which get deleted.

### Method 2: separate tab 

The bug can also be triggered by opening a new browser tab and navigating to localhost with a path to a non-existent page, like `localhost:8501/foobarbaz`, and then closing the tab quickly just as it starts to load.

This takes several attempts as it seems to depend on the timing of when the new tab is closed. This method reproduces the issue about 10% of the time, 

Possibly related (which was never solved): #7199

### Other observations

- If one creates a new cookie using devtools with a random name, that cookie is _not_ deleted by the login flow. It is only the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie that is deleted.
- The issue seems to only occur on Chrome and Edge, but not on Firefox. This might be due to differences in how closed connections are handled, or perhaps differences in timings.

title: Provide a way to specify the starting port number for the free port search
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Our IT department configured a range of ports for our use, from _N_ to _N_+100.

When I specify `--server.port N`, Streamlit tries only this single port; it does not continue looking for the next available port in the range.

This enhancement request is for a `--server.port.from` option that would start the search at the specified port.

### Why?

Currently we resort to `netstat` or grepping `ps` to find a port to use.

### How?

A `--server.port.from` command-line option would be consistent with the existing `--server.port` option. Or, a `--server.port.search` (or similar) Boolean option could provide control over whether search is performed with the existing `--server.port` option.

### Additional Context

comments.text:
@user I think this is intended behavior. If I specify in a config that I want the software to use a specific port, I don't want it choosing a different port on me. you already pointed out you can find out which ports in a machine are in use. 

If you don't specify a port in the config, then I believe streamlit will start searching for a port counting up from 8501; this may be sufficient for your use case.

Thanks for the reply, @user!

Indeed, the default port search does start from 8501, and that is workable for now. But we also have non-Streamlit applications using the same port range, 8501-8599 port range, and so it would be nice to be able to specify the starting point for Streamlit's port search.

body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I would love to have an option to schedule an app reboot in the community cloud. This could be linked to displaying a status/alert in the app that it will reboot in X time.

### How?

title: Ability to set cookies
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I use Streamlit 1.34.0, for me the only possible way to get/set cookies was to run JS inside Streamlit using this package: https://github.com/toolittlecakes/streamlit_js

While we got `st.cookies` in version 1.38.0, I would love Streamlit to natively support setting cookies from client or the server side, I assume there is some functionality allowing this, given it's already able to set an XSRF cookie.

### Why?

People might want to add their own cookies for performance, auth, tracking/marketing etc - in my use case it was for a custom made authentication.

With the hacky workaround I found, getting and setting cookies were extra "components" that required separate keys & occupied some space in the page. Having a simpler & visually non-obtrusive way would be better.

In the workaround I also have to wait until the cookies I set propagate - making me run a `sleep` and run my `get_cookies` function again until the change propagates.

### How?

We can use a function `st.set_cookie` where we would define all the parameters for the cookie we'd like to set.

Given Streamlit has already a way to set cookies internally, just like it sets the xsrf cookie we can generalize that functionality to setting any cookie.

### Additional Context

I'd be happy to help with the implementation, though I'll have to check my employer first on open source contributions + acquaint myself a bit with the codebase

comments.text: Duplicate of #861

Hey, thanks for the request! There's already an old issue for this, I think we can keep the discussion in there. Please feel free to upvote or comment! I'll also change the title of that issue to more accurately reflect that it's about writing cookies now that we have the ability to read cookies. 

We indeed want to add support for writing cookies but it could take us a while to get there because a) we're mostly focused on adding built-in authentication at the moment (which is obviously very related to cookies!) and b) writing cookies comes with some security and legal questions that we need to figure out (e.g. do we also need to offer a cookie banner component). 

You're welcome to build a prototype and I'll have a look at it (best to post it on the other issue and mention me), but please keep in mind that even if the quality of the PR is good, we won't be able to merge it until we figure out the API and security/legal questions.

comments.text:
Hi @user thanks for submitting this issue. It seems there's two problems:
1) putting your db connection is session_state isn't the best place for that kind of thing to live. I'd take a look at [`st.connection`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/connections/st.connection) instead
2) this has uncovered an issue with how were measuring memory for session_state as part of our metrics

I'll keep this issue open to track (2), but would recommend you trying (1) to see if it can unblock you.

Fixed by #15334 (merged 2026-05-27). The cache/stats sizing path now goes through a `safe_sizeof()` guard (`lib/streamlit/runtime/stats.py`) that catches the `TypeError: cannot create weak reference` raised when sizing SQLAlchemy objects, so the `/_stcore/metrics` endpoint no longer 500s. (As an extra layer, #15472 also made the expensive memory stats off by default.)

Closing as resolved — please reopen if it recurs on a current release.

title: Allow streamlit app to be run as a normal python script with `python app.py`
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

It would be convenient to allow users to simply run `python streamlit_app.py`, without having to necessarily run `streamlit run streamlit_app.py`

### Why?

This would make it easier to launch streamlit apps in a more flexible way. My particular interest is being able to do `uv run streamlit_app.py` and use [inline script dependencies](https://peps.python.org/pep-0723/) to share completely standalone single-file streamlit apps that don't require any setup other than installing uv.

This can be accomplished today by adding some code that grabs the streamlit internal method that gets run with `streamlit run` and calling that directly, but it would be much nicer if this was the default behavior:

The dependencies above were inserted to the script automatically with:
```sh
uv add --script app.py yfinance
uv add --script app.py streamlit
```

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = [
#     "streamlit",
#     "yfinance",
# ]
# ///

import streamlit as st
import yfinance as yf

msft = yf.Ticker("MSFT")

# get all stock info
st.write(msft.info)

# Hacky stuff required to be added to make it work without `streamlit run`:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import get_script_run_ctx
    if get_script_run_ctx() is None:
        from streamlit.web.cli import main
        import sys
        sys.argv = ['streamlit', 'run', __file__]
        main()
```

As-is, this works simply by:
1. Installing uv
2. Running `uv run app.py`

No other setup is needed at all.

### How?

`python streamlit_app.py` or `python -m streamlit_app` just work, automatically calling the `main` function if streamlit is imported in them.

### Additional Context

  File ".../streamlit/commands/navigation.py", line 190, in navigation
    if page._default:

```

> [@user](https://github.com/sgrimee) I just tested it with [this multi-page app example](https://github.com/Sven-Bo/streamlit-multipage-app-example) and it worked fine. I'll be happy to take another look if you can provide a reproducible example.

yes, it works. thanks!

A caveat related to using 3rd party components: ensure you import any 3rd party components **after** doing `streamlit.web.bootstrap.run`. This is because when a component is declared, which typically happens when they're imported, it requires a `ScriptRunContext` (at least on 1.45.0), which is populated by the bootstrap code. A failure to do so will result in the component being replaced by a warning along the lines of:

>Your app is having trouble loading the **st_custom_component.some_comp** component.
>
>If this is an installed component that works locally, the app may be having trouble accessing the component frontend assets due to network latency or proxy settings in your app deployment.
>
>For more troubleshooting help, please see the [Streamlit Component docs](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/custom-components) or visit our [forums](https://discuss.streamlit.io/).

To summarize:

```python
from st_custom_component import some_comp  # <<<<<<< BAD

def main():
    some_comp()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "__streamlitmagic__" not in locals():
        from streamlit.web.bootstrap import run

        run(__file__, False, [], {})

    main()
```
```python
def main():
    from st_custom_component import some_comp  # <<<<<<< GOOD

    some_comp()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "__streamlitmagic__" not in locals():
        from streamlit.web.bootstrap import run

        run(__file__, False, [], {})

    main()
```

It runs properly with uv, but I see this warning message

```
Thread 'MainThread': missing ScriptRunContext! This warning can be ignored when running in bare mode.
```

This is how I end up with.

Instead of merging main python script file and streamlit entrypoint file, I separated those into two dedicated files.

```python
# app/main.py
from streamlit.web import bootstrap

from app import entrypoint

def streamlit_run(flag_options):
    """simplified version of `streamlit.web.cli._main_run()`"""

    bootstrap.load_config_options(flag_options=flag_options)
    bootstrap.run(entrypoint.__file__, False, [], flag_options)
    # you can of course just hard-code the streamlit entrypoint file path instead:
    # bootstrap.run("app/entrypoint.py", False, [], flag_options)

def main():

    # setup global states like shared loggers here

    streamlit_run({
        # NOTE: hard-coded streamlit options
        #       we can't use streamlit environment variables because we are bypassing
        #       `streamlit run` command and directly calling `bootstrap.run()` to set global loggers.
        "browser.serverAddress": "localhost",
        "server.address": "0.0.0.0",
        "server.headless": True,
    })

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# entrypoint.py

# streamlit entrypoint file.
# can be executed with `streamlit run entrypoint.py`
# though you might loose some global states then

def main():
    import streamlit as st # put this under `main()` so that it won't be executed on `import app.entrypoint`

    pg = st.navigation([
        st.Page("../pages/1_first_page.py"),
        st.Page("../pages/2_second_page.py"),
    ])
    pg.run()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Still compatible with `uv`.

If anyone's trying to register project entry point to use with `uv`, i.e. 
```toml
[project.scripts]
my_dashboard = "my_package.my_dashboard.main:main"
```
you'll need to put the workaround in a function and replace `locals` with `globals`:
```python
def main() -> None:
    if "__streamlitmagic__" not in globals():   # <<<<< changed here
        from streamlit.web.bootstrap import run

        run(__file__, False, [], {})

    # Rest of your init code
```
Then it's possible to do `uv run my_dashboard`. HOWEVER, I am yet to find a way to get it to automatically switch to the `my_package/my_dashboard` subfolder (I don't want to specify this in the run command), so if you have a `.streamlit` folder with configs/secrets, it **won't be picked up** unless you `cd` to the app's directory manually beforehand.

I'll reach out to Astral and update.

## Update

This use case is addressed by the new `st.App(...).run()` API shipping in Streamlit 1.59.

This gives Streamlit apps an officially supported Python entry point, so launcher files can be run directly with:

```bash
python app.py
uv run app.py
```

It also works well with PEP 723 inline script dependencies, e.g. a launcher can declare `streamlit` and app-specific dependencies directly in the file and be run with `uv run app.py` without a separate environment setup step.

Example:

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#   "streamlit",
#   "yfinance",
# ]
# ///

import streamlit as st

app = st.App("streamlit_app.py")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```

This avoids relying on internal `streamlit.web.bootstrap` calls. The supported pattern is a small Python launcher that points at the Streamlit app script, rather than making arbitrary Streamlit scripts auto-run themselves.

I checked this with the latest streamlit-nightly and it works great -- thanks @user!

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#   "streamlit-nightly>=1.58.1.dev20260616",
#   "yfinance",
# ]
# ///

import streamlit as st

app = st.App("streamlit_app.py")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```
@user one minor thing -- this doesn't open the browser automatically -- is there a workaround for that?

title: Streamlit slows down with many nested blocks
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

In [this forum discussion](https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/dialog-doesnt-open-a-second-time/79808/10?u=raethlein), we investigated an issue where a user app became slower after release 1.35.

It looks like the CSS styling introduced [in this PR 5](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/commit/d7caf46e15bedf39194eb4e0216122fd67bc1b41#diff-f07ff4b4a42b5e81423c56b26dd51c5ecfea90bf6a477dbe59aa86d423d2122dR91-R107) is problematic and started to make rendering bigger apps using many blocks way slower.

### Reproducible Code Example

### Steps To Reproduce

The issue can be reproduced by running the user's app from this repo: https://github.com/diogovalentte/mantium/tree/main
via Docker locally. The user has provided a database than can be copied to the postgres container in order to populate the app with enough data. I assume you could reproduce it with a simpler Streamlit app, but I haven't found the time yet.
However, when running the app with Streamlit 1.34 and with 1.38 you can notice a significant scroll speed difference even up to a point in which the app freezes. If you comment out the CSS selector from the linked lines of code above, the issue seems to be fixed.
Here are a few example commands (update the paths) where you can easily make the changes locally on your Mac and copy them into the container to test changes:

```bash

# [On your local Mac] 
## Build the frontend
cd frontend
yarn build

## copy the build artifacts into the container
docker cp ~/Projects/streamlit/frontend/app/build/ mantium-dashboard:/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/streamlit/static/

## Open bash in container
docker exec -it mantium-dashboard /bin/bash  

# [In container]

## Remove the current frontend assets
rm -rf /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/streamlit/static/*

## Move the copied-from-Mac frontend assets into the container
mv /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/streamlit/static/build/ /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/streamlit/static
```

### Expected Behavior

Scrolling through the app should not make the browser window freeze and/or be super slow.

### Current Behavior

- [X] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

- Browser:

title: Multiple custom Streamlit components fail to load in deployed environments
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Several custom Streamlit components, including `streamlit_shadcn_ui`, `st_bridge`, `st_aggrid`, `streamlit_image_select`, and `st-theme`, fail to load in deployed environments (except Streamlit Community Cloud), though they work correctly in local development. The issue seems related to network latency or proxy settings affecting frontend asset access in the deployment environment.

Examples were people -including me- have such problems:

* https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/button-in-your-app-is-having-trouble-loading-the-streamlit-shadcn-ui/75962
* https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/need-help-with-streamlit-bridge-on-hf-space/105889
* https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/trouble-loading-the-st-aggrid-aggrid-component/75480
* https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/streamlit-image-select-image-select-component-issue/74615
* and lastly it happens to my deployment in Google Cloud Run with st-theme component

### Reproducible Code Example

I haven't been able to reproduce the issue locally; it only occurs when I deploy it to Google Cloud Run. Could this be due to the serverless nature of the platform, where multiple container instances are spun up to serve the streamlit app? I've read that using **session affinity** (https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/session-affinity) in Google Cloud Run deployments is recommended to ensure requests are routed to the same instance, especially since Streamlit relies on WebSockets. Could this be causing the problem? Does Streamlit really needs such a feature to work correct?

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Deploy the app on a cloud platform (e.g., Google Cloud Run).
2. Include any of the mentioned custom components (streamlit_shadcn_ui, st_bridge, st_aggrid, etc.).
3. Run the app and observe the error when trying to load the components.
4. See the error message indicating trouble loading the frontend assets for the components.

### Expected Behavior

The app should load the custom components without any issues, just as it works in local development. The frontend assets should be accessible in the deployment environment.

### Current Behavior

When deploying the app, the custom components fail to load. The error message indicates that the app is having trouble accessing the component frontend assets, which may be due to network latency or proxy issues. The components work fine locally but fail when deployed.

Your app is having trouble loading the `[component_name]` component.

If this is an installed component that works locally, the app may be having trouble accessing the component frontend assets due to network latency or proxy settings in your app deployment.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.38.0
- Python version: 3.10
- Operating System: Docker container based on python:3.10-slim
- Browser: All

### Additional Information

title: Native `uv` support in Community Cloud
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Streamlit Community Cloud installs dependencies with `uv`, but if I use `uv` natively to manage packages in my project it's not actually compatible with Cloud (since it uses a different `pyproject.toml` format than poetry). Instead, I have to keep a separate requirements.txt file just for community cloud, which is annoying!

### Why?

I should be able to use a `pyproject.toml` and/or `uv.lock` file in my repository and have it work with Streamlit Community Cloud.

Today Community Cloud doesn't recognize the `uv.lock` file, and if it sees `pyproject.toml` it assumes the Poetry format. However, Poetry's format is actually different from the standard Python one (see https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/writing-pyproject-toml/ ). Note, this could actually be a problem for projects that use other package managers (including pip!) with the [more modern and preferred](https://www.stuartellis.name/articles/python-modern-practices/#use-a-pyprojecttoml-file) pyproject.toml format

### How?

An ideal solution which would help all package managers is to differentiate pyproject.toml with the Poetry format vs the Python native format, and use an appropriate tool depending on which is used.

A simpler workaround (which would at least solve my use case 😅) is to look for a `uv.lock` file in the repo and install with that instead when present, such as using `uv sync --frozen`

### Additional Context

Example forced workaround: https://github.com/JoshuaC215/agent-service-toolkit/blob/main/requirements.txt
Also came up here: https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/install-dependencies-in-streamlit-cloud-based-on-uv-pyproject-toml/79557
Relevant Streamlit docs cite: https://docs.streamlit.io/deploy/streamlit-community-cloud/deploy-your-app/app-dependencies#other-python-package-managers

title: Command line flags for common arguments
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I am proposing that we implement flags for common CLI arguments.
Currently, config options can be configured as outlined [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/cli/run).

### Why?

A simple flag system would be more memorable and terse, align more with common CLI conventions, and reduce typing errors for frequently used options.

### How?

Running in headless mode `--headless` or `-h` for `--server.headless true`
Rerunning on save `--run-on-save` or `-r` for `--server.runOnSave true`
Specifying a port `--port <number>` or `-p <number>` for `--server.port <port number>`

This would transform the current

> `streamlit run <entrypoint file> --server.headless true --server.runOnSave true --server.port 6000`

into the proposed

> `streamlit run -h -r -p <port number> <entrypoint file>`

### Additional Context

title: Activate virtual env when doing `streamlit run`, similar to `uv run`
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

[uv](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) automatically activates a virtual environment in the current dir when using `uv run` (which just runs a normal Python script, i.e. `uv run script.py` is roughly equivalent to `python script.py`). Maybe we should do the same thing for `streamlit run`?

### Why?

Don't need to think about activating the correct venv anymore. Especially if you're using `uv` for installation, this is pretty neat. 

### How?

Not sure if we'd want to do this for every env or only for ones managed by `uv`. Could also look into how `uv run` does this under the hood so we can do it in a safe way. See [here](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/python/uv/__main__.py) for example.

comments.text:
Hey, thanks for the feedback! 

The deploy button will only show up if you access an app on localhost, e.g. during development. If you deploy an app somewhere (no matter if Community Cloud or your own server) and access the app via a non-localhost URL, the deploy button should not show up (with exactly the reasoning that it would be confusing for non-technical viewers!). Can you describe your deployment setup and in which situation the deploy button is bothering you?

Btw you can already hide the entire toolbar at the top right with the config option `client.toolbarMode`, see [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/configuration/config.toml). If there are enough upvotes, we might consider adding another config option specifically for the deploy button!

> I get streamlit is linked to a private org. And that private org needs to push for it's profit.
But that should never go against the open source mission of st.

No worries, we are 100% committed to open source :) The deploy dialog also links to other deployment options than Streamlit Community Cloud (agree we need better documentation for this though!) and Community Cloud is a completely free product, we don't make any profit from it.

To be clear: you can hide only the development options (including the deploy button) with `cient.toolbarMode="viewer"`. As @user mentioned, the deploy button only shows up in "development mode" when accessing the app from `localhost`. Even then, the configuration option can force it into "viewer mode."

Without setting the configuration option, it's in "auto" mode.
```
# Change the visibility of items in the toolbar, options menu,
# and settings dialog (top right of the app).
# Allowed values:
# * "auto"      : Show the developer options if the app is accessed through
#                 localhost or through Streamlit Community Cloud as a developer.
#                 Hide them otherwise.
# * "developer" : Show the developer options.
# * "viewer"    : Hide the developer options.
# * "minimal"   : Show only options set externally (e.g. through
#                 Streamlit Community Cloud) or through st.set_page_config.
#                 If there are no options left, hide the menu.
# Default: "auto"
toolbarMode = "auto"
```

this did the trick for me: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/configuration/st.set_option

```
import streamlit as st
st.set_option("client.toolbarMode", "viewer")
``` 

pro tip for the previous (incomplete) answers: give context for the people reading your posts. also, preferably indicate references like official documents.

@user To clarify for posterity, the `st.set_option` command is typically used if you don't have access to set the app's configuration or if you need to change that option at runtime. Otherwise, the best practice is to set it through [`config.toml`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/configuration/config.toml) as linked jrieke's post.

@user Just to confirm if you're encountering a bug that needs to be reported (or if you specifically need to hide the deploy button while keeping other developer options visible):

When you access an app through localhost (and don't configure the toolbar mode), it will display in "developer" mode which includes the deploy button. (This is what "auto" does: assumes you're developing the app if you access it through localhost.)

[image]

However, if you configure the toolbar mode to "viewer" this should go away without any CSS hacks.

[image]

In your working directory, all you (should) need is a `.streamlit/config.toml` file with:

```toml
[client]
toolbarMode = "viewer"
```

```python
import streamlit as st

st.write(f"The app is being accessed through URL: {st.context.url}")
toolbar = st.get_option("client.toolbarMode")
st.write(f"Toolbar mode is set to: {toolbar}")
```
The `toolbarMode` does work, apologies.  I had tried this but I think it was in conjunction with an older config example.   Thanks.

I'm looking into resolving this feature request. I think we have three options:
1. Improve documentation of `client.toolbarMode="viewer"` to specify that this will also hide the deploy button and that the deploy button is only shown when developing on localhost.
2. Add a dedicated `client.showDeployButton` / `client.hideDeployButton` option.
3. Introduce a `client.showStreamlitBranding` / `client.hideStreamlitBranding` that could potentially be used to hide other Streamlit-branding-related aspects as well like the version number. 

cc @user

## Update

We improved the `client.toolbarMode` documentation to specify that `client.toolbarMode="viewer"` will enforce that the `deploy` button is always hidden.

title: Add Custom File Path to Watcher which is outside the path of the main script
body:
**PR open**: #[9656](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/9656)

### Checklist

### Summary

Add a feature to allow watching a custom path in Streamlit, enabling the application to monitor all files within that directory and its subdirectories. Currently, Streamlit supports a blacklist for excluding paths but lacks an option to specify a custom path to be watched in full.

### Example Scenario:

```bash
/home/<user>/
├── streamlit_project/
│   ├── main_app.py
│   ├── data/
│   │   └── local_data.csv
└── shared_data/
    └── external_data.csv
 ```

### Why?

The current system only supports watching the directory of the main streamlit script or excluding certain files via a blacklist. In cases where projects have structured directories or additional assets in specific folders, it is important to have the flexibility to define custom paths for Streamlit to watch, ensuring that all relevant files are reloaded as needed. This would improve developer experience by allowing greater control over what Streamlit monitors for changes, preventing unnecessary reloads and improving workflow.

### How?

The implementation introduces a new configuration option, `server.customWatchPath`, which allows users to specify a custom path for Streamlit to monitor. This path will be recursively watched for changes to any files within it. The main changes in this implementation are:

1. **Configurable Option**: A new option, `server.customWatchPath`, is added in the `config.py` file. This allows users to define a custom directory for file watching through Streamlit's configuration system.

~~2. **Runtime and Path Watching**: The runtime has been updated to store the `custom_watch_path` in the `RuntimeConfig`. The path watcher (`EventBasedPathWatcher`) has been extended to accept this custom path and watch it recursively for any file changes. If a custom watch path is provided, the watcher registers it and logs relevant debug information about the additional path being watched.~~

3. **Recursive Directory Watching**: In `local_sources_watcher.py`, the `_register_watcher` method has been updated to handle directory watching, ensuring that all files within the custom path are monitored for changes. If the custom path is valid, it will be registered with the path watcher, and any file changes within the directory will trigger a file change event.

These changes allow for a flexible approach where users can monitor any directory, ensuring that all necessary files are captured without relying solely on the default Streamlit watch settings.

### Additional Context

You can find other users expressing a similar needs in the streamlit discussion threads below:

- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-monitor-the-filesystem-and-have-streamlit-updated-when-some-files-are-modified/822/21
- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/watching-custom-folders/1507
- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-extend-streamlit-watchers-to-monitor-custom-user-files/36694/2

**Note**:  

Streamlit offers the ability to allow users to watch modules in the PYTHONPATH as seen in #845 , but this method requires modifying the PYTHONPATH, which some users may find undesirable. Allowing a custom path to be specified provides a more flexible solution without requiring any changes to the PYTHONPATH, ensuring a smoother experience for users who may have structured directories outside of the default Python paths.

comments.text:
@user Thanks for raising the issue. I might have a theory as to why this happens: I think using `st.pyplot` within a `st.cache_data` might be a bit problematic. If `st.pyplot` is used within an `st.cache_data` the element message will get cached globally. But the pyplot message only contains a link to the plot image that is stored in our internal media storage. The image in the media storage gets cleaned up when the session disconnects. So if you disconnect a session and connect a new one, it will receive the cached pyplot message, but the image does not exist anymore in storage. 

As a workaround, you can move the `st.pyplot` call out of the cached function and only return the matplotlib object from the function. Does that solve the issue?

Hey @user Appreciate the issue. Matplotlib is a bit finnicky in a web server. I believe it's tied to (See https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/user_interfaces/web_application_server_sgskip.html and https://matplotlib.org/3.3.2/faq/howto_faq.html#working-with-threads). Likely, you may need to save the chart as an image and utilize `st.image`

We do have some recommendations in our [docs](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/charts/st.pyplot) to handle this perhaps better. Have you tried these?

@user 

No I don't believe I've tried any of those work arounds. I also didn't realize that matplotlib could be that tricky in a webserver.

With that being said, I'm sorta finished with the [project](https://cij-analysis.streamlit.app/) that I was working on that had this problem. So I don't know if I'll put any more effort into fixing this issue for now. I actually just put a big message above the problem plots saying: **(If the plots below don't load, try refreshing the page.)**

Should I keep this issue up?

title: Allow streamlit apps to easily serve robots.txt at the root level
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I'd like for there to be an easy and straightforward way to serve a robots.txt file at the root level directory of a dockerized streamlit app.

### Why?

I recently deployed a dockerized streamlit app on GCP’s Cloud Run service and I’ve been getting bombarded with requests from OpenAI’s GPTBot at the rate of about 1req/s for the last several hours. I’d like to prevent them from continuing to hit my app so naturally I’d like to serve a robots.txt at the root level, but I don’t know how do this with streamlit and I’m not finding anything in the documentation about robots.txt.

I looked into the static file serving part of the documentation, but it only serves files at /app/static/robots.txt and not at the root level. Given that streamlit likely takes over routing, I'm wondering if there's even exists a non-hacky way of serving the robots.txt at the root level of a streamlit app.

### How?

The robots.txt file should be accessible in a format like this: https://my-streamlit-app.com/robots.txt

### Additional Context

Link to discussion on streamlit forum: https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-serve-robots-txt/83548

comments.text:
Update: I moved my dockerized streamlit [app](https://jreadability-demo.streamlit.app/) off of GCP and onto streamlit cloud to prevent incurring further costs.

After opening this issue, I decided to leave my app up for a total of two weeks just to see if/when the bots would stop. Unfortunately they didn't and here's the final results:
[image]

It cost nearly $3 a day for the first week, so over $20 and it's still costing around $1 a day to keep up!

To those reading this and wondering why the bots seem to find my innocent streamlit app so interesting, I suspect that it might have to do with the fact that I shared it on [reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/LearnJapanese/comments/1g3kjy0/i_built_a_japanese_readability_calculator_in/) and it was moderately popular in a specific subreddit for about a day. Scraper bots love using reddit for training data and I think my app was basically caught in the crossfire, with no means of protection (robots.txt).

## Update

Exciting news 🎉 Starting with **Streamlit 1.53**, we've added experimental support for custom HTTP routes via the new ASGI/Starlette integration.

You can now serve `robots.txt` at the root level:

```python
from streamlit.starlette import App
from starlette.routing import Route
from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse

async def robots_txt(request):
    return PlainTextResponse(
        "User-agent: *\n"
        "Allow: /\n"
        "Disallow: /admin/\n"
    )

app = App("main.py", routes=[Route("/robots.txt", robots_txt)])
```

Run with `streamlit run myapp.py` and `robots.txt` will be served at the root.

We'd love your feedback on this feature! Please try it out and report any issues in our [feedback thread](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13600).

> **Note:** Requires `pip install streamlit[starlette]`

## Update

Starlette will become the default server in 1.57 which will allow serve a robots.txt file as described above without having to install the `starlette` dependencies. The `App` object will also be available in the `st` namespace:

```python
import streamlit as st

...

st.App(...)
```

title: Unable to upload files due to both AxiosError (Network and 403)
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I'm using streamlit [`1.38.0`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/releases/tag/1.38.0) with python [`3.10.3`](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3103/) and I can't upload files in my hosted app (which is deployed with Kubernetes). The deployment is orchestrated through a `.gitlab-ci.yml` file that runs two pipelines: **package** (which downloads packages and creates directories based on a `Dockerfile`) and **integration** (which handles the actual deployment of the application).

Here is a snippet of the relevant part of my `Dockerfile` (last version after many tries):
```bash
COPY . .

RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt

EXPOSE 8080

HEALTHCHECK CMD curl --fail http://localhost:8080/_stcore/health

ENTRYPOINT ["streamlit", "run", "app.py", "--server.port=8080", "--server.address=0.0.0.0", "--server.enableXsrfProtection=false"]
```
*FYI, in the `.streamlit/config.toml` file, I set the same options with the same values in the entrypoint above.*

The application runs fine but I literally can't upload any files at all (of any type, `.zip`, `.pdf`, `.xlsx`, `.csv`, ...) . For example:
- for `.xlsx` files, I receive the `AxiosError: Network Error`
- for `.csv` files, I receive the `AxiosError: Request failed with status code 403`

I've already tried every suggested solution I could find in similar posts (github, streamlit forum, stackoverflow, reddit, ..), most of which recommend turning off *CORS* and *XSRF* protection (with `"--server.enableCORS=false", "--server.enableXsrfProtection=false"`) but none have worked for me. I also tried the streamlit documentation's recommended [fix](https://docs.streamlit.io/knowledge-base/deploy/remote-start#symptom-3-unable-to-upload-files-when-running-in-multiple-replicas), yet still same problem.

There are also some posts discussing downgrading to version [`1.29.0`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/releases/tag/1.29.0) (released in November 2023) but that's not an option for me as it would break a significant part of my code. Also, I'm not even sure if downgrading would resolve the issue. It's not worth the risk, TBH.

Our current Kubernetes `virtualService` configuration is as follows:
```yaml
virtualService:
  enabled: true
  gateway: dep-default-gateway
  hosts:
    - xxxxxx-dep-default-gateway.xxxxx.xxxxx.pack
    - xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.com (yellow address in the images)
```
Do you please have a solution adapted to my use case? I'm really out of ideas and I don't master nor understand any of these technologies: CORS, XSRF, Cookies, Proxy, Kubernetes, and Docker. I'm just a Python developer and a streamlit lover.

title: Allow `packages.txt` inside a folder on Community Cloud
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

To install packages via `apt-get` on Community Cloud, you can add a `packages.txt` file to the repo, see [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/deploy/streamlit-community-cloud/deploy-your-app/app-dependencies#apt-get-dependencies). However, this file always needs to be at the root of the repo. Other dependency files (e.g. `requirements.txt`) can also be inside folders, and Cloud searches from the dir of the main app file up to the root for these dependency files. It would be great to add the same mechanism for `packages.txt`. 

### Why?

If you have multiple apps in a repo in different folders, it's pretty annoying if the `packages.txt` file needs to be at the root of the repo and its contents are getting installed for every single app. 

### How?

Use the same search mechanism that we use for `requirements.txt` and other dependency files. If there's a `packages.txt` at the same level as the main app file use that. If not, move up to the parent folders and search for `packages.txt` there until the root is reached. 

### Additional Context

[global]

title: Makefile fails when Python is not detected; add missing prompt and Python version check
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Adding a check at the top of Makefile for the PYTHON_VERSION variable. If the variable is empty, display a clear and informative message to the user.

### Why?

Here is the relevant part in the Makefile:

```Makefile
# Make uses /bin/sh by default, but we are using some bash features.  On Ubuntu
# /bin/sh is POSIX compliant, ie it's not bash.  So let's be explicit:
SHELL=/bin/bash

INSTALL_DEV_REQS ?= true
INSTALL_TEST_REQS ?= true
USE_CONSTRAINTS_FILE ?= true
PYTHON_VERSION := $(shell python --version | cut -d " " -f 2 | cut -d "." -f 1-2)
GITHUB_REPOSITORY ?= streamlit/streamlit
CONSTRAINTS_BRANCH ?= constraints-develop
CONSTRAINTS_URL ?= https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/${CONSTRAINTS_BRANCH}/constraints-${PYTHON_VERSION}.txt

# Black magic to get module directories
PYTHON_MODULES := $(foreach initpy, $(foreach dir, $(wildcard lib/*), $(wildcard $(dir)/__init__.py)), $(realpath $(dir $(initpy))))
```

When I use `make all-devel` command to compile, I forgot to activate the Python virtual environment, which caused the system to not detect the Python version. The `PYTHON_VERSION` variable became empty, resulting in the following error

I believe it is helpful to add a check for the `PYTHON_VERSION` variable and inform the user, especially when using a Python virtual environment. This will allow for quick identification of the error cause, rather than encountering connection errors.

### How?

The solution can be very simple. For example you can add these lines to detect the `PYTHON_VERSION` variable.

```Makefile
# Make uses /bin/sh by default, but we are using some bash features.  On Ubuntu
# /bin/sh is POSIX compliant, ie it's not bash.  So let's be explicit:
SHELL=/bin/bash

INSTALL_DEV_REQS ?= true
INSTALL_TEST_REQS ?= true
USE_CONSTRAINTS_FILE ?= true
PYTHON_VERSION := $(shell python --version | cut -d " " -f 2 | cut -d "." -f 1-2)
GITHUB_REPOSITORY ?= streamlit/streamlit
CONSTRAINTS_BRANCH ?= constraints-develop
CONSTRAINTS_URL ?= https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/${CONSTRAINTS_BRANCH}/constraints-${PYTHON_VERSION}.txt

# Black magic to get module directories
PYTHON_MODULES := $(foreach initpy, $(foreach dir, $(wildcard lib/*), $(wildcard $(dir)/__init__.py)), $(realpath $(dir $(initpy))))

ifeq ($(strip $(PYTHON_VERSION)),)
    $(error "Error: Python version is not detected. Please ensure Python is installed and accessible in your PATH.")
endif

To be clear, for this you only need `max_header_size` or both `max_header_size` and `max_body_size`?

1. What are the default values for these options in Tornado?
2. Can you research what the possible security implications of changing these options are and write a short text here? I guess it should be fine since it's something developers explicitly need to set and we can add a warning to the docstring. But I'd like to at least have a short investigation and have our security team give this a quick review. 
3. My biggest concern is probably that we were thinking a few times about getting rid of Tornado at some point and switching to a more modern alternative like Starlette. Can you do some quick research on whether these (or similar options) are also supported in Starlette?

Will check Tornado default values for this args and we can set them as defaults in streamlit.
I will also check the other http server as well.

Regarding **Tornado**
**max_header_size** default value is **65536**
**chunk_size**  default value is **65536**
**max_body_size** default value is **None**

Regarding **Starlette**
in my opinion it is not good for Streamlit. It doesn't have any limits incorporated so without Nginx in front of it it basically open hole.
Discussion regarding limiting request size started April 2020 and until now not resolved
https://github.com/encode/starlette/discussions/1516

There is another option if you really want to change Tornado to something different.
It is **Sanic Framework** with very good configuration
https://sanic.dev/en/guide/running/configuration.html#builtin-values

I'm not sure what is your timeline of going away from Tornado but I propose to implement changes I did myself for my internal project and set default **Tornado** values.

Let me know

Re the migration to another framework, that's definitely a longer-term thing (~years). 

Can you still answer these 2 questions:
- To be clear, for this you only need max_header_size or both max_header_size and max_body_size?
- Can you research what the possible security implications of changing these options are and write a short text here? I guess it should be fine since it's something developers explicitly need to set and we can add a warning to the docstring. But I'd like to at least have a short investigation and have our security team give this a quick review.

To have streamlit app receiving long urls it is enough to set **max_header_size** for Tornado HTTPServer
[this test shows failing long url with default settings](https://github.com/mysiar/tornado/blob/streamlit_tests/tornado/test/httpserver_streamlit1_test.py)

[this test shows working long url max_header_size = 2MB](https://github.com/mysiar/tornado/blob/streamlit_tests/tornado/test/httpserver_streamlit2_test.py)

As for security implications I do not think that it actually makes application not secure, it is just size difference and will be used only in case someone hit limitations like I have in my apps.

So this is basically it.
Now question is if you want this change to be implemented in streamlit server?

Hey, we're planning to start a project to migrate from Tornado to Starlette in May, so until that's done we don't want to expose these type of config options.

Starlette will become the default server in 1.57 and Tornado will be removed as a dependency.

title: Implement browser session API
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

Browser sessions allow developers to track browser status in streamlit, so that they can implement features like authentication, persistent draft or shopping cart, which require the ability to keep user state after refreshing or reopen browsers.

### Why?

The current streamlit session will lost state if users refresh or reopen their browser. And the effort of providing a API to write cookies has been pending for years. I think provide a dedicated API to track browser session would be cleaner and easier to implement.  
With this API developers don't need to know how it works, it can be based on cookie or local storage or anything else. And developers can use it with singleton pattern to keep state for browser to persist whatever they want in streamlit.

### How?

This feature will introduce several new APIs:
* `st.get_browser_session(gdpr_consent=False)`, which will set a unique session id in browser if it doesn't exist, and return it.
If `gdpr_consent` is set to True, a window will pop up to ask for user's consent before setting the session id.
* `st.clean_browser_session()`, which will remove the session id from browser.

The below is a POC of how `get_browser_session` can be used to implement a simple authentication solution:

```python
from streamlit.web.server.websocket_headers import _get_websocket_headers
from streamlit.components.v1 import html
import streamlit as st

from http.cookies import SimpleCookie
from uuid import uuid4
from time import sleep

def get_cookie():
    try:
        headers = st.context.headers
    except AttributeError:
        headers = _get_websocket_headers()
    if headers is not None:
        cookie_str = headers.get("Cookie")
        if cookie_str:
            return SimpleCookie(cookie_str)

def get_cookie_value(key):
    cookie = get_cookie()
    if cookie is not None:
        cookie_value = cookie.get(key)
        if cookie_value is not None:
            return cookie_value.value
... [18 lines trimmed] ...
    return st.session_state['st_session_id']

@st.cache_resource
def get_auth_state():
    """
    A singleton to store authentication state
    """
    return {}

st.set_page_config(page_title='Browser Session Demo')
session_id = get_browser_session()

auth_state = get_auth_state()
if session_id not in auth_state:
    auth_state[session_id] = False

st.write(f'Your browser session ID: {session_id}')

if not auth_state[session_id]:
    st.title('Input Password')
    token = st.text_input('Token', type='password')
    if st.button('Submit'):
        if token == 'passw0rd!':
            auth_state[session_id] = True
            st.rerun()
        else:
            st.error('Invalid token')
else:
    st.success('Authentication success')
    if st.button('Logout'):
        auth_state[session_id] = False
        st.rerun()
    st.write('You are free to refresh or reopen this page without re-authentication')
```

A more complicated example of using this method to work with oauth2 can be tried here: https://ai4ec.ikkem.com/apps/op-elyte-emulator/ 

### Additional Context

Related issues:
* https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/861
* https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8518

title: file_uploader headers on https deployed streamlit app
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

When using `file_uploader` component on a streamlit application that has been deployed behind a load balancer that performs https termination everything works fine.

Let's suppose that my application is accessible through `https://myapp.com`
`enableCors`and `enableXsrfProtection`are both on.

Then due to this block in the `upload_file_request_handler.py` file:
```
if config.get_option("server.enableXsrfProtection"):
            self.set_header(
                "Access-Control-Allow-Origin",
                server_util.get_url(config.get_option("browser.serverAddress")),
            )
            self.set_header("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "X-Xsrftoken, Content-Type")
            self.set_header("Vary", "Origin")
            self.set_header("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true")
``` 

If I let my configuration unchanged everything works fine , but we will have 
` Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with localhost as value which is something I don't want to have.

If I put `myapp.com` as `browser.serverAddress` , I'll get http://myapp.com (and not https://myapp.com) in the ` Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header

and if i enter `https://myapp.com` as `browser.serverAddress` it will be `http://https://myapp.com` in the ` Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header.

If we look at `server_util.get_url` we can understand this behavior , as I said in the beginning I perform https termination before the application and therefore I don't set any `server.sslCertFile` that will make the `get_url ` adding https as protocol instead of http.

Finally I don't even understand why we set this Cors header in the file_uploader, in any of the scenario everything works fine (except that we have weird  ` Access-Control-Allow-Origin`: the whole point of my issue) , because I guess when using the file_uploader, requests are made from the same origin and aren't cross origin requests.

title: Page Reload on Cache Miss
body:
### Checklist

### Summary

I am noticing behaviour very similar to the behaviour described in [this issue](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9036#issuecomment-2594452089) when using v1.41.1. In particular, I'm noticing that if I cause a rerun by pressing "R" and there is a cache miss, then sometimes the page reloads, element status is lost (e.g. active element, but not state like selected items) and scroll position is lost (the page is scrolled to the very top).

I first noticed this on a large page with many elements and several cached_data references. I was able to narrow it down to a single simple page show in the reproducible code.

The problem seems to come up when there are multiple cached_data functions that all expire together and all need to be run again as part of the same app rerun.

The attached video shows the reload happening consistently on the cache miss, i.e. every 3 seconds. I've found that if I reduce the number of cached_data functions, then this is less likely to happen.

### Reproducible Code Example

[[image]](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-10199)

```Python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

@st.cache_data(ttl=3, show_spinner=True)
def get_table(table_name: str) -> list:
    return [{"name": "AUD"}, {"name": "USD"}, {"name": "EUR"}, {"name": "GBP"}]

sections.summary:
I am noticing behaviour very similar to the behaviour described in [this issue](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9036#issuecomment-2594452089) when using v1.41.1. In particular, I'm noticing that if I cause a rerun by pressing "R" and there is a cache miss, then sometimes the page reloads, element status is lost (e.g. active element, but not state like selected items) and scroll position is lost (the page is scrolled to the very top).

I first noticed this on a large page with many elements and several cached_data references. I was able to narrow it down to a single simple page show in the reproducible code.

The problem seems to come up when there are multiple cached_data functions that all expire together and all need to be run again as part of the same app rerun.

The attached video shows the reload happening consistently on the cache miss, i.e. every 3 seconds. I've found that if I reduce the number of cached_data functions, then this is less likely to happen.
